 SCHENECTADY — After a three-hour meeting, the city council failed to agree on breaking the tax cap, halting the budget process and pushing the budget past the charter-designated deadline.
 The council recessed the meeting until Thursday at 5:30 p.m.
 “What are we doing?” Council President Carl Williams asked as council members tried to find another day to vote through its 2027 budget.
 He was one of four council members who agreed to break the tax cap, which restricts how high municipalities can raise taxes. Typically, the number is around 2%. But in order to go over the tax cap, the council needed a supermajority of five votes.
 Throughout the evening, the council appeared to reach an agreement on a 15% tax increase. No one on the council was happy about it. Councilmembers John Mootooveran and Kim Wiggins both would not move over a 13% increase, but the finance committee agreed to move both the tax cap and budget resolutions forward.
 The council deliberated for about two hours before moving the resolutions forward. It then took a 45-minute break for the finance department to prepare the budget with the amendments, Assistant Corporation Counsel Sean O’Brien explained.
 When the group returned around 8:20 p.m., the first vote was the tax cap resolution. Councilmembers Mootooveran, Wiggins and Justin Chaires all voted against breaking the tax cap.
 Williams replied, “no comment,” before entering a private office immediately after the meeting. Mootooveran, Wiggins and Chaires also could not be reached for comment before entering a private office.
 However, Councilmember Hayden Engert had a strong opinion about what had happened during the 45-minute break to change the presumed outcome of the night.
 “Tomorrow is a big day in the City of Schenectady. I would say there is a reason I’m supporting Ms. [Rachel] Ward [for city council],” he said, referencing Election Day and the race between Ward and Chaires for his city council seat. “I think that after tomorrow, I would be quoted on the record saying that we will have a budget by the end of the week.”
 Engert, Williams and Councilmembers Doreen Ditoro and Carmel Patrick all agreed to break the tax cap. Patrick was visibly and audibly shocked when the tax cap vote failed.
 “What happened?” she said. “I thought we were all in agreement.”
 Ditoro expressed similar thoughts after the meeting. Mayor Gary McCarthy had one word for what had happened in the council room.
 “Lunacy.”
 McCarthy vetoed the first budget the council passed in 2025 and refused to sign the second budget because of his disagreement with the document. He would not have vetoed the 15% agreement the council came to on Monday, he said after the meeting.
 If it had passed, the budget would have increased taxes by $408 for a house assessed at $200,000. It would be a far cry from the original 42.5% proposed, but the council was also banking on $6.5 million more in “anticipated state aid.”
 The meeting will reconvene on Thursday.
 Schenectady County reporter Erica Bouska can be reached at ebouska@dailygazette.net .
